newsitem.title: USA: Florida Panthers aiming for Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Florida Panthers aiming for Wall Street.

text.p: The Florida Panthers hockey team is taking a shot at Wall Street this week as its successful owner Wayne Huizenga takes the team public in a $73 million offering of stock to financial investors and fans.
The Panther's weak financial record should be outshined by its smashing team record, analysts say, and the Midas touch of Huizenga.
He built the video chain, Blockbuster Entertainment, controls Republic Indutries Inc, and owns the Miami Dolphins football team and the Florida Marlins baseball team.
"This deal has lots of sex appeal because of the team and Huizenga, but it's losing money so we'll see how it trades," said Barbara Bradley, managing director of syndicate at Laidlaw Equities Inc.
The Panthers, formed only three years ago, had a 12-game unbeaten streak until last week. In 1995, the team went to the Stanley Cup finals, but lost to the Colorado Avalanche.
"We think this team is several years away from profitability, if at all, so this is a real leap of faith," said the IPO Insider report.

The company has never posted a profit in three years of operation and revenues have been jagged, cut sharply in fiscal 1995 by the hockey strike. For fiscal 1996, which ended in June, the company lost $25 million on revenues of $33 million.
Cash flow is also negative, with a deficit of $55.4 million at June 30, 1996, meaning it could need more capital infusions, according to a regulatory filing.
If investors are willing to ignore the losses, and some are, the hat trick for the Panther's IPO could be the short supply of stock being offered.
Parent company Florida Panthers Holdings Inc will offer 4.6 million of the total 7.3 million shares to private investors, leaving only 2.7 million shares for the market to squabble over.
"Given the expected interest and demand by individual fans, we would not be surprised by near-terms gains. Offered at $10, it will reach at least $15," the IPO Insider said.

The Class A shares will be sold at $10 each and will trade on the Nasdaq under the symbol "PUCK." About 60 percent of the company will be sold off, although Huizenga will keep voting control of the Panthers through a second class of stock to abide by NHL rules.

One critical issue for the team is the completion of its new Broward County Civic Arena in time for the 1998-1999 season. Until it moves out of its current small Miami Arena, the team says it will continue to post yearly losses of at least $20 million.

Currently the only other publicly traded sports team is the Boston Celtics LP, which trades at about 8 times earnings. There have also been published reports that George Steinbrenner might be considering taking the New York Yankee baseball team to market.
